q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: James I and his son Charles I both believed in the 'Divine Right of Kings': the idea that the king was directly appointed by God to rule. They thought that the king should be able to act without having to seek approval from Parliament.
o: The Divine Right of Kings held that the king was directly appointed by God to rule
The Divine Right of Kings held that Parliament appointed the king

q.t: For how long did Charles I rule without Parliament before he was forced to recall it?
q.e: When he could not get Parliament to agree with his religious and foreign policies, he tried to rule without Parliament at all. For 11 years, he found ways in which to raise money without Parliament's approval but eventually trouble in Scotland meant that he had to recall Parliament.

q.t: What happened when Charles I entered the House of Commons to arrest five parliamentary leaders?
q.e: Charles I entered the House of Commons and tried to arrest five parliamentary leaders, but they had been warned and were not there. No monarch has set foot in the Commons since.
o: They had been warned and were not there
Parliament voted to hand them over

q.t: Which TWO names were given to the sides in the English civil war?
q.e: Civil war between the king and Parliament could not now be avoided and began in 1642. The country split into those who supported the king, the Cavaliers, and those who supported Parliament, the Roundheads.

q.t: At which TWO battles was the king's army defeated in the English civil war?
q.e: The king's army was defeated at the Battles of Marston Moor and Naseby. By 1646, it was clear that Parliament had won the war.

q.t: What title was Oliver Cromwell given as leader of the new republic?
q.e: After his campaign in Ireland and victory over Charles II at Worcester, Cromwell was recognised as the leader of the new republic. He was given the title of Lord Protector and ruled until his death in 1658.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Charles II famously hid in an oak tree after his defeat at Worcester.
q.e: Cromwell defeated this army in the Battles of Dunbar and Worcester. Charles II escaped from Worcester, famously hiding in an oak tree on one occasion, and eventually fled to Europe.

q.t: From which country did Parliament invite Charles II to return in May 1660?
q.e: In May 1660, Parliament invited Charles II to come back from exile in the Netherlands. He was crowned King Charles II of England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland.

q.t: What does the Latin phrase 'habeas corpus' mean?
q.e: The Habeas Corpus Act became law in 1679. Habeas corpus is Latin for 'you must present the person in court'. The Act guaranteed that no one could be held prisoner unlawfully. Every prisoner has a right to a court hearing.
o: You must present the person in court
The king is subject to the law

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: During Charles II's reign, in 1665, there was a major outbreak of plague in London. The following year, a great fire destroyed much of the city, including many churches and St Paul's Cathedral.
o: The plague in London came before the great fire
The great fire of London came before the plague

q.t: Who designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the great fire?
q.e: London was rebuilt with a new St Paul's, which was designed by a famous architect, Sir Christopher Wren. Samuel Pepys wrote about these events in a diary which was later published and is still read today.

q.t: What is the Royal Society, formed during the reign of Charles II?
q.e: Charles II was interested in science. During his reign, the Royal Society was formed to promote 'natural knowledge'. This is the oldest surviving scientific society in the world. Among its early members were Sir Edmund Halley and Sir Isaac Newton.
o: The oldest surviving scientific society in the world
The oldest theatre company in Britain

q.t: Which of these is NOT a responsibility of an MP, as listed in the handbook?
q.e: MPs represent everyone in their constituency, help to create new laws, scrutinise and comment on what the government is doing, and debate important national issues.

q.t: Until 1958, which TWO groups sat in the House of Lords alongside hereditary peers?
q.e: Until 1958, all peers were 'hereditary', which means they inherited their title, or senior judges, or bishops of the Church of England.
o: Bishops of the Church of England

q.t: What changed for hereditary peers in 1999?
q.e: Since 1999, hereditary peers have lost the automatic right to attend the House of Lords. They now elect a few of their number to represent them in the House of Lords.
o: They lost the automatic right to attend the House of Lords
They were all removed from the House of Lords permanently
They were given the right to stand for the House of Commons
They gained the power to overrule the Commons

q.t: Who formally appoints life peers?
q.e: Since 1958, the Prime Minister has had the power to nominate peers just for their own lifetime. These are called life peers. Life peers are appointed by the monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister.
o: The monarch, on the advice of the Prime Minister
The Speaker of the House of Commons
The House of Commons by a vote

q.t: How many members are there in the Scottish Parliament?
q.e: The Scottish Parliament was formed in 1999. It sits in Edinburgh. There are 129 members of the Scottish Parliament (MSPs), elected by a form of proportional representation.

q.t: How many Assembly Members does the National Assembly for Wales have, and how often are elections held?
q.e: The Welsh government and National Assembly for Wales are based in Cardiff. The National Assembly has 60 Assembly members (AMs) and elections are held every four years using a form of proportional representation.

q.t: Which TWO matters remain under central UK government control rather than being devolved?
q.e: Policy and laws governing defence, foreign affairs, immigration, taxation and social security all remain under central UK government control. However, many other public services, such as education, are controlled by the devolved administrations.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Since 2011 the National Assembly for Wales has been able to pass laws on its 20 devolved topics without the agreement of the UK Parliament.
q.e: The Assembly has the power to make laws for Wales in 20 areas, including education and training, health and social services, economic development, and housing. Since 2011, the National Assembly for Wales has been able to pass laws on these topics without the agreement of the UK Parliament.

q.t: In which building do members of the Scottish Parliament meet?
q.e: In Scotland the elected members, called MSPs, meet in the Scottish Parliament building at Holyrood in Edinburgh.

q.t: Where are the official reports of proceedings in Parliament published?
q.e: Proceedings in Parliament are broadcast on television and published in official reports called Hansard. Written reports can be found in large libraries and at www.parliament.uk.

q.t: What does it mean to say the UK has a free press?
q.e: The UK has a free press. This means that what is written in newspapers is free from government control. Some newspaper owners and editors hold strong political opinions and run campaigns to try to influence government policy and public opinion.
o: What is written in newspapers is free from government control
Newspapers are given away without charge
Newspapers may not express political opinions
Newspapers are funded by the television licence

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: By law, radio and television coverage of the political parties must be balanced and so equal time has to be given to rival viewpoints. Newspapers, by contrast, are free of government control and their owners may run campaigns.
o: Radio and television coverage of the political parties must be balanced by law
Newspaper coverage of the political parties must be balanced by law
